title: Speke's Journeys in Search of the Source of the Nile
intro: John Hanning Speke, an English army officer, went to East Africa with Richard Burton to find the Great Lakes rumoured to lie in the centre of the continent, in the hope of locating the source of the Nile. He later returned with James Augustus Grant, and most of the day to day work was done by a large labour force of porters, soldiers, guides and cooks.
ending: Speke and Grant reached Gondokoro in January 1863 and arrived in England in June 1863. Burton disputed that the Nile had been traced, and Speke died on 15 September 1864, the day before a planned debate with him.

legs.title: With Burton to Lake Tanganyika and Lake Victoria, 1857 to 1859

stops.text: Speke and Burton began their inland journey from Zanzibar Island in June 1857. They stayed at the residence of Atkins Hamerton, the British consul.
stops.quote: The journey, which started from Zanzibar Island in June 1857, where they stayed at the residence of Atkins Hamerton, the British consul

stops.text: By 7 November 1857 they had travelled over 600 miles on foot and donkey and reached Kazeh, a settlement of Arab slave traders. There they rested; Burton became gravely ill and Speke went temporarily blind as they went on west.
stops.quote: By 7 November 1857, they had travelled over 600 miles on foot and donkey and reached Kazeh (Tabora), where they rested and recuperated among Arab slave traders who had a settlement there.

stops.text: The two arrived at Ujiji in February 1858 and became the first Europeans to reach Lake Tanganyika, though Speke was partly blind and could not properly see it. Burton was too ill to explore the lake, so Speke crossed it with a small crew and canoes.
stops.quote: After an arduous journey, the two arrived in Ujiji in February 1858 and became the first Europeans to reach Lake Tanganyika

stops.text: The caravan halted again at Kazeh on the way back. Burton was too weak to go on to a second lake, so he stayed in base camp while Speke made a 47-day side trip with 34 men, Bombay and Mabruki as his captains.
stops.quote: They had also heard of a second lake to the north-east, and in May 1858, they decided to explore it on the way back to the coast. But Burton was too weak to make the trip and thus stayed in base camp when the main caravan halted again at Kazeh.

stops.text: After Speke's side trip, which reached Lake Victoria on 30 July 1858, the return journey to the coast began from Kazeh on 26 September 1858 with 152 porters. Both men were often ill and some of the way were carried in a litter.
stops.quote: On 26 September 1858 the return journey from Kazeh was started with 152 porters

stops.text: From the coast they went by ship to Zanzibar and then to Aden. Burton was not granted a medical certificate to travel, so Speke left alone on HMS Furious and reached England on 8 May 1859.
stops.quote: Once Speke and Burton were back on the coast they went by ship to Zanzibar and then travelled to Aden. Once in Aden, Burton was not granted a medical certificate to travel and thus Speke left on HMS Furious

legs.title: With Grant to Buganda and down the Nile, 1860 to 1863

stops.text: Speke and James Augustus Grant left Portsmouth on 27 April 1860 and set out from Zanzibar in October 1860. Locals often fled or fought, taking them for slavers, and demands for gifts and passage fees delayed them and used up their supplies.
stops.quote: Together with James Augustus Grant, Speke left Portsmouth on 27 April 1860 and departed from Zanzibar in October 1860.

stops.text: After reaching Lake Victoria on 28 July 1862, Speke went round its western side and, on the north side, found the Nile flowing out of it at the Ripon Falls. He had also stayed at the court of Muteesa I, Kabaka of Buganda.
stops.quote: but on the north side of the lake, Speke found the Nile flowing out of it and discovered the Ripon Falls.

stops.text: Speke, reunited with Grant, travelled down the Nile but could not map all of its flow from the lake. They reached Gondokoro in January 1863, where he met Samuel Baker. The Pethericks, sent by the Royal Geographical Society to meet them, were away trading ivory.
stops.quote: By January 1863 Speke and Grant reached Gondokoro in Southern Sudan, where he met Samuel Baker and his "wife".

stops.text: Speke continued to Khartoum by Baker's ship. From there he sent a telegram to London reading "The Nile is settled." Burton replied that Speke had not followed the river from the lake to Gondokoro, so could not be sure it was the same river.
stops.quote: Speke, via Baker's ship, then continued to Khartoum from which he sent a celebrated telegram to London: "The Nile is settled."

notes: Lake Victoria and Lake Tanganyika are lakes and the article names no town or camp at Victoria on either trip, so Victoria is not a stop; it is mentioned in the texts of Kazeh and Ripon Falls. Speke's 30 July 1858 side trip is one 47-day excursion from Kazeh (no turning place named). The Aden stop has no date in the article (Speke reached England on 8 May 1859). The Ripon Falls stop has no date in the article; the article gives June 1862 for leave from Muteesa but the order is odd: it says Speke reached the lake on 28 July 1862 yet leave from Muteesa in June 1862 and 'divorced' in April 1862, so the article contradicts itself on 1862 dates; I used neither date for the falls. Buganda's court has no named town in the article, so it is left out as a stop. Stop texts for the falls mention Muteesa and Buganda from the article. Speke's second-leg route by Karagwe is not named. Africans named: Sidi Mubarak Bombay and Mabruki, captains of the first journey, not given stops of their own. 'Discovered the Ripon Falls' in the quote is the article's wording; the text says 'found'.
